levels.title: Few New Facts
levels.story: Rowan pins a fact sheet to the last tree. "A state is only worth keeping if it teaches us something new," says Rowan. Kit crosses off every clearing that shows nothing the search has not seen before.

everyday.scene: When you skim the news, you skip a story if it holds no fact you have not already read. You keep only the pages that add something.
everyday.question: How can a planner skip most states and still find a plan?
everyday.answer: It keeps a state only if it makes some fact, or small set of facts, true for the first time. Everything else is dropped without being explored.

lessons.title: Novelty
text: Novelty asks what is new about a state. A state has novelty 1 if it contains a fact that no earlier state had. It has novelty 2 if no single fact is new, but some pair of facts has not appeared together before. Otherwise its novelty is higher.

Say Kit has already seen the starting state, the Bridge state and the holding-p state. A new state with Kit at the Bridge holding p has no new single fact, but the pair 'Kit at Bridge' and 'Kit has p' is new. Its novelty is 2.

terms.meaning: The size of the smallest set of facts in a state that has never appeared together in an earlier state.

lessons.title: IW(1) and IW(2)
text: Iterated width, written IW(k), is breadth-first search that drops any state whose novelty is bigger than k. IW(1) keeps a state only if it brings a brand-new fact.

text.text: So IW(1) keeps at most one state per fact, because each state it keeps must make some fact true for the first time. Kit's world has 11 facts, so at most 11 states. IW(2) also keeps states with a new pair, at most 11 + 55 = 66.

terms.meaning: Breadth-first search that drops states with novelty above k.

lessons.title: Fast but incomplete
text: Pruning is risky: IW(1) can drop a state the plan needs. In Kit's world it finds 'Kit at Dock' in 2 moves, but it cannot make 'p at Dock' true. Carrying p across the Bridge shows no new single fact, so the state is dropped.
IW(2) finds the 4-action plan for 'p at Dock'. Width-based planners run searches like these, and they work because many planning problems need only a small k.

deeper.title: Both goals together
text: In Kit's world, IW(2) solves 'p at Dock' and 'q at Cabin' one at a time, but fails when both must be true together.

Nothing is left on the frontier, and 'p at Dock' never appeared. IW(1) has failed on this goal. IW(2) also keeps states with a new pair, and it finds the 4-action plan.

activities.prompt: Put the steps of IW(1) in order.
items: Put the start state on the frontier
Take the oldest state off the frontier
Make each state its actions lead to
Keep a new state only if it has a fact never seen before
Repeat until the goal appears or nothing is left
hints: It is breadth-first, so the oldest state goes first.
Pruning happens after a state is made.

summary: You measured how novel a state is, saw IW(1) and IW(2) drop states with too little that is new, and watched IW(1) get stuck when a plan needed a state with no new single fact.
Rowan folds the fact sheet. "Fast, but not always right." Kit adds it to the notebook. "Like a guess I have to double check."

mistake.title: Thinking pruning is free
mistake.text: Dropping states makes a search fast, but a dropped state may be the one the plan needs. IW(1) is quick but incomplete, so planners try larger k when it fails.
